extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian aesthetics/teleology) and natural scientists interested in the epistemology of teleological judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and judge natural things (especially organised beings) with respect to purposiveness (teleology), distinguishing reflective vs determinant judgements and the proper regulative role of teleology within natural science. The page supplies conceptual criteria, maxims, and critiques of systems that try to explain purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal form as basis for judging a natural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a thing as a natural purpose on account of its internal form: the specific organisation (internal form) of a thing suffices for our faculty of judgement to regard its origin as possible according to the rule of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the internal organisation of a blade of grass justifies, for human judgement, considering its origin according to purposive rules even though this does not establish a final purpose of nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposive references are only hypothetical (not categorical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging purposiveness from external relations (uses by other beings) yields only hypothetical purposive references and does not establish a categorical purpose of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: grass serving oxen which serve men does not establish that men must exist as a final purpose; such chained external relations point beyond empirical teleology to a supersensible ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Reason as a regulative maxim (not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the maxim that 'everything in the world is some way good for something; nothing is vain' as a regulative principle of Reason to guide reflection on nature, not as an objective constitutive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle justifies expecting purposiveness in nature as a heuristic for investigation, but it is a subjective maxim of reflective judgement rather than proof of design or an objective principle of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use teleological judgement only as regulative/clue, not as proof of design
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological (purposive) judgements provide a regulative method or clue for investigating natural phenomena and must not be treated as establishing a designed purpose or a supernatural cause within natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'wisdom', 'economy', or 'forethought' of Nature are permissible as analogies for investigation, but must not be taken to ascribe an intelligent architect to inanimate matter; teleology supplements mechanical investigation without replacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce theological principles as internal principles of natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science must not take concepts (e.g., God or a divine architect) that belong outside it as domestic (internal) principles, because this produces circularity and mixes the boundaries of sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing God into natural science to explain purposiveness, then using that purposiveness to prove God, is a delusive circle; keep theology and empirical natural science distinct in method and grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mechanical causality; use final causes only supplementarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate natural phenomena according to mechanical causality first; the principle of final causes is a different investigatory mode used only to supplement mechanical explanations where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological reflection should not prejudice mechanical causality — one should pursue mechanical laws 'as far as we can' and use teleological considerations to extend inquiry where mechanism seems inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply teleological judgement particularly to organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological mode of judging is especially necessary and permissible for a particular class of objects—organised beings—because their internal organisation appears explicable only by reference to final causes for the purpose of understanding their constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleology is an unavoidable mode for understanding the constitution of organisms through observation, but its use is restricted to appropriate objects and remains a reflective (subjective) principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective judgement needs necessary maxims and may produce antinomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reflective judgement must subsume under laws not yet given, it requires necessary maxims to guide reflection; these maxims can conflict, producing a dialectical antinomy that must be diagnosed and resolved critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'natural Dialectic' is an unavoidable illusion stemming from the nature of cognitive faculties and must be exposed in critical reflection instead of being turned into dogmatic assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: First maxim (regulative): always reflect by mechanical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulative maxim: all production of material things and their forms must be judged possible according to merely mechanical laws (i.e., always attempt mechanical explanation first).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not deny other modes of reflection; it prescribes that investigation begin with mechanical principles so that proper empirical knowledge of nature is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second maxim (regulative): some products may require final causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulative maxim: some products of material nature cannot be judged possible according to merely mechanical laws and require reflection according to the principle of final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mechanical reflection cannot account for certain natural forms (especially purposive organisation), Reason is entitled to adopt teleological reflection as a guiding idea without asserting it as an objective determinant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the two maxims as regulative, not constitutive (avoid antinomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two maxims are converted into constitutive (objective) principles about the possibility of objects, they contradict each other and produce an antinomy; instead they must remain regulative guiding-methods of reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining the regulative status preserves the compatibility of mechanical investigation and teleological reflection and prevents illegitimate metaphysical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reflecting, hypothesis of an intelligent cause is a permissible Idea, not an objective assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: For reflective judgement it is correct to think of a causality distinct from mechanism (an intelligent cause acting according to purposes) as an Idea to guide reflection; for determinant judgement asserting this as objective is unprovable and dogmatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any appeal to a supreme Understanding as a heuristic Idea for reflection on purposiveness, keeping open mechanical explanations and avoiding dogmatic claims beyond experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish designed (technica intentionalis) vs undesigned (technica naturalis) Technic of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide nature's 'Technic' (productive power in accordance with purposive rules) into: designed (technica intentionalis) — implying a particular kind of causality acting with design; and undesigned (technica naturalis) — essentially akin to mechanical causality, where purposiveness is a subjective condition of judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps clarify whether purposiveness is to be explained by intentional causality or as a product of nature's mechanism coupled with our mode of judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and critique explanatory systems for purposiveness (Idealism vs Realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broad families: Idealism of purposiveness (purposiveness is undesigned — e.g., chance/casuality or Spinozist fatality) and Realism of purposiveness (some purposiveness is designed — e.g., hylozoism or theism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page sketches critiques: Epicurean chance fails to explain the illusion; Spinozist fatality reduces purposiveness; Hylozoism is circular (derives life from organised matter known only by experience); Theism cannot dogmatically establish the possibility of natural purposes for the determinant judgement — thus none fully accomplishes what they promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatic treatment of the concept of a natural purpose (use critical procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat the concept of a thing as a natural purpose dogmatically (i.e., as subsumed under a determinant principle of Reason); instead consider it critically in reference to our cognitive faculties and as an empirically conditioned concept used regulatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogmatic use would demand assurance of objective reality; critical use recognizes the concept's empirical conditioning and limits it to a maxim of judgement rather than an ontological claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek teleological explanations even for apparently purposeless or unpleasant phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that phenomena unpleasant or contrary to purpose (vermin, mosquitoes, dreams) may have purposive roles when viewed teleologically—for example, motivating cleanliness, prompting environmental improvements, or serving remedial functions during sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such examples to show teleological judgement can yield entertaining or instructive insights that mere physical observation might miss; but keep such teleological explanations tentative and reflective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider beauty as objective purposiveness linked to cognitive faculties' free play
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of nature can be regarded as a kind of objective purposiveness insofar as it connects with the free play of human cognitive faculties in apprehending and judging appearances, contributing to a sense of respect and ennoblement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aesthetic purposiveness helps justify the Idea of nature as a system of purposes that includes humans as members, but it remains within the reflective judgement's regulative use.
